overview: Franche-Comté was the historic County of Burgundy, east of the separate Duchy of Burgundy. During this map’s 1650 to 1715 span it passed from the Spanish Habsburg monarchy into France. French conquest in 1674 was confirmed by the 1678 Treaty of Nijmegen. The continuing outline after that treaty represents a French province, not an independent country surviving until 1715, and is smaller than today’s combined Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region.

periods.title: A contested Habsburg county
periods.summary: War brought a temporary French occupation in 1668 and a lasting conquest in 1674.

periods.title: Conquest and French provincial government
periods.summary: The 1678 peace confirmed the county’s transfer to France; the map continues into its provincial history.

sections.title: War, government and a hilltop fortress

items.text: France conquered Franche-Comté briefly in 1668 and again in 1674. Royal intendants subsequently supervised justice, policing and finance. A change of ruler therefore affected taxes, officials and the handling of disputes, not only the name at the top of a map.

Fort Belin guarded the approaches to Salins, a town whose salt industry made it especially valuable. After the 1674 surrender, Vauban was asked to rebuild the local defences, including Belin, Bracon and Saint-André. Fortifying the hills linked military engineering to protecting an important working town.

Salins made salt by heating naturally salty water until the water evaporated. Workers fed fires beneath large pans, originally using wood; coal belonged to later developments. Unlike a sunny coastal salt pond, this inland industry depended on fuel, heat and repeated skilled work.

Women worked at several stages of salt production, including gathering, drying and packing it. Female supervisors could direct both women and men. Helpers were often relatives, such as daughters or husbands. Family life and industrial work could be closely connected inside these crowded, demanding workplaces.

An earlier seventeenth-century custom gave a worker a birth bonus of about 25 kilograms of salt. That was useful household wealth in an age when salt mattered for cooking and preserving food. The custom predates this layer’s 1650 start, giving background to the workers’ longer history.

sections.title: Bread, pipes and a fountain without wine

items.text: In September 1686, Besançon’s officials confronted complaints about dreadful bread. The intendant opposed leaving public baking to a tiny group of contractors and wanted other bakers invited to compete. The surviving record documents the argument; it does not prove that every loaf immediately improved.

A fountain inspection later that month found water disappearing at the springs and through defective pipes. Reliable public water required people to inspect and maintain the whole route. A handsome fountain was less useful if the water escaped before reaching its spout.

Celebrations for the birth of the Duke of Berry in 1686 included fireworks. Officials refused to let wine flow from a fountain, however, because of the disorder this could cause. Apparently the party planners had reasons to keep that particular tap firmly closed.

The university, founded at Dole in 1423, moved to Besançon in 1691. Its subjects included law, medicine and theology. The transfer changed where generations of future lawyers and other educated professionals studied, and shifted an important institution between two rival regional towns.

The university initially rented three rooms in a Carmelite monastery. Temporary arrangements proved remarkably durable. In 1701, theology professor Jean Girard’s donation helped establish a library. University life could begin with borrowed space and gifts of books, rather than a magnificent purpose-built campus.

Saint-Jacques Hospital’s pharmacy moved into its new setting in 1705. It included a dispensing area, a laboratory and an office, and also supplied people outside the hospital. Preparing medicines required equipment, storage and skilled work as well as a doctor’s prescription.

Hospital gardens completed in 1702 provided fresh air and medicinal plants. A clock installed in 1703 helped organise remedies and religious observances. These small arrangements reveal how patients’ days were structured, from time outdoors to scheduled care.

The hospital also had a coercive role. Its 1685 royal charter authorised confinement and work for poor people and beggars. Care and control could occupy the same institution, so its history includes restrictions on vulnerable people as well as treatment.

A scholarly transcription of the gate inscription reads “Tibi derelictus est pauper”: “The poor person is entrusted to you”. The iron gate was installed in 1703; the one displayed today is a replacement copy. This short Latin appeal asked visitors to think about responsibility for people needing help.

ending.text: The 1678 treaty confirmed French possession. Franche-Comté continued as a province, while its towns and institutions retained their histories. The imported 1715 endpoint is a map cutoff, not the disappearance of the region.
